title: Taika Waititi Fires Back at “Klara and the Sun” Critics, Calls Them Irrelevant “Sad Lost Souls” – No Reviews Read in 15 Years.
body:
Taika Waititi has taken to Instagram to push back against the wave of criticism surrounding his latest film, *Klara and the Sun*. The New Zealand‑born director, whose name has become synonymous with off‑beat humor and heartfelt storytelling, dismissed the negative reviews as “irrelevant” and labeled the detractors “sad lost souls” in a candid post that quickly went viral. While the movie’s opening weekend box‑office numbers have fallen short of expectations, Waititi’s defiant response underscores a growing tension between creators and the relentless churn of modern criticism.

The Instagram post, which featured a still from the film’s climactic scene, was accompanied by a terse caption: “I haven’t read a review in 15 years. I listen to the people, not the press.” By framing the debate as a clash between “the people” and “the press,” Waitti​i positioned himself on the side of audience sentiment, even as early audience scores on aggregators such as Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic mirrored the tepid critical response. The film, an adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel, explores the bond between a solar‑powered android and a young girl in a near‑future world. Critics have praised its visual design but have been divided over its pacing and emotional resonance, leading to a mixed‑to‑negative consensus that has weighed on its commercial performance.

Industry observers note that Waitti​i’s outburst is not an isolated incident. In recent years, high‑profile directors—from Christopher Nolan to Greta Gerwig—have publicly questioned the influence of traditional film criticism, especially as social media amplifies audience voices. The shift reflects a broader democratization of opinion: streaming platforms, fan forums, and real‑time comment sections now shape a film’s reputation as quickly as any newspaper review. Yet, the backlash against Waitti​i also reveals the delicate balance creators must strike. While bypassing the press can rally a loyal fan base, it risks alienating the very critics whose analyses often guide undecided moviegoers.

Box‑office data for *Klara and the Sun* paints a stark picture. In its domestic debut, the film earned roughly $4 million, a figure that falls well below the $12 million benchmark set by Waitti​i’s previous successes such as *Thor: Love and Thunder* and *Jojo Rabbit*. International markets have shown modest interest, with limited releases in Europe and Asia contributing another $2 million. Analysts attribute the underperformance to a combination of factors: the film’s niche sci‑fi premise, competition from summer blockbusters, and the lingering effects of pandemic‑era audience fatigue. Moreover, the timing of the release—just weeks after the highly anticipated return of a major franchise—may have siphoned potential viewers.

Despite the numbers, Waitti​i’s public stance could have a silver lining. By championing “the people,” he taps into a growing sentiment among younger audiences who feel disconnected from elite criticism. In the weeks following his post, social media hashtags praising the film’s themes and aesthetic trended on Twitter, and fan‑generated content—ranging from TikTok edits to fan‑art—has begun to circulate more widely than traditional promotional material. This grassroots buzz, while unlikely to overturn the opening‑week box‑office deficit, may extend the film’s lifecycle on streaming platforms, where word‑of‑mouth can translate into sustained viewership.

Looking ahead, the episode raises questions about the evolving power dynamics in the entertainment ecosystem. As filmmakers like Waitti​i continue to leverage direct communication channels, the traditional gatekeeping role of critics may further erode, prompting a re‑evaluation of how success is measured. For now, *Klara and the Sun* remains a polarizing entry in Waitti​i’s oeuvre—celebrated by some for its visual ambition and dismissed by others for its narrative choices. Whether the director’s defiant message will reshape audience perception or simply add another chapter to the ongoing dialogue between art and critique remains to be seen, but it undeniably highlights the increasingly personal nature of modern film discourse.
